stops.name: Freiberg (Příbor), Moravia: the wool merchant's house
stops.campa: In a rented room on the Schlossergasse, above a locksmith's shop in the small Moravian town of Freiberg, Amalia Freud bears her first son to the wool merchant Jakob Freud, twenty years her senior. They name him Sigismund Schlomo. Jakob already has two grown sons from an earlier marriage; the infant's nephew John, older than his uncle, will be his first playmate and rival. The caul he is born in is kept by his mother as a talisman of destined greatness, the first of many signs she reads into her golden-haired boy.

stops.name: Vienna, Leopoldstadt: the family settles
stops.campa: The wool trade fails and the family drifts, first to Freiberg, then a year in Leipzig, before Jakob Freud brings his household to Vienna's Leopoldstadt, the crowded Jewish quarter across the Danube Canal. They take rooms on the Pfeffergasse, one of the poorer streets; Sigmund, not yet four, will grow up amid peddlers and pawnshops within sight of the Prater's chestnut avenues. He will call himself, all his life, a Viennese who never forgot he was first a stranger there, the immigrant's watchfulness folded permanently into the future doctor's eye.

stops.name: Vienna, the Prater: the wandering poet's prophecy
stops.campa: At a restaurant garden in the Prater, where Viennese families take their Sunday air among the chestnuts, a wandering poet earns his supper improvising verses about the diners' children. He comes to the dark-haired boy Amalia calls her little Moor and, warming to the game, declares that this one will grow up to sit in the cabinet of ministers. The family repeats the story for decades, half in jest, half in earnest, the household's own small oracle, spoken over a boy who will indeed rule an empire, though not the one the poet meant.

stops.name: Vienna: the Matura and Goethe's 'Die Natur'
stops.campa: First in his class through eight years at the Sperlgymnasium, the boy who once devoured Cervantes and taught himself Spanish for the pleasure of it now stands at the door of a profession. At a public lecture near the end of his schooling he hears Professor Carl Brühl read aloud the incomparably beautiful essay on Nature attributed to Goethe: a hymn to a Nature that creates and devours without pause or pity. The reading decides him on the spot: he will abandon the law he had half-intended and study medicine, to serve that same devouring, creating force from the inside.
stops.quote: Nature! We are surrounded and embraced by her — powerless to leave her, and powerless to enter her more deeply.
stops.quote_source: 'Die Natur' (attrib. Goethe/Tobler), recalled by Freud as decisive, An Autobiographical Study (1925)

stops.name: Trieste: the eel gonads
stops.campa: Sent by his zoology professor Carl Claus with a government grant, the nineteen-year-old medical student spends four weeks at the marine station of Sant'Andrea, slicing open some four hundred eels in search of the male reproductive organ that has eluded naturalists since Aristotle. He finds, in one specimen, the lobed structure he seeks hidden in the abdominal cavity, confirms what a Polish zoologist had already glimpsed, and writes his first scientific paper. It settles nothing large, but it teaches him the discipline of looking hard at what nobody else has bothered to dissect.

stops.name: Vienna: the medical degree
stops.campa: Three years late by his own exacting standard, distracted by physiology under Ernst Brücke, by philosophy, by a hundred tributary interests, Freud is finally awarded the degree of Doctor of Medicine by the University of Vienna. He has no taste for general practice and would rather stay in Brücke's laboratory forever measuring nerve fibers, but the physiology institute has no post to give him and poverty presses. He takes a position at the General Hospital instead, the reluctant first step from pure research toward the clinical work that will, without his yet suspecting it, remake the century's idea of the mind.

stops.name: Paris, La Salpêtrière: Charcot's clinic
stops.campa: On a travel grant Freud crosses to Paris and spends the winter at the Salpêtrière, the great asylum-hospital where Jean-Martin Charcot, the Napoleon of the neuroses, demonstrates hysteria before crowded amphitheaters as though it were a disease of the nerves like any other, produced and abolished under hypnosis at his command. Freud watches spellbound, translates Charcot's lectures into German, and objects once, timidly, that a theory being tested does not quite fit the facts observed. Charcot's answering shrug becomes the sentence Freud will repeat for the rest of his life, against every objector to what he is about to discover.
stops.quote: Theory is good, but it doesn't prevent things from existing.
stops.quote_source: Charcot, as recalled by Freud in On the History of the Psycho-Analytic Movement (1914)

stops.name: Vienna: the private practice opens
stops.campa: Back from Paris and burning with Charcot's example, Freud opens a private practice for nervous diseases on the Maria-Theresien-Strasse, resigning his hospital post to earn, at last, enough to marry. He advertises electrotherapy and hypnotic suggestion, the fashionable tools of the trade, though he privately suspects both will fail him; his real instrument is still being forged, in the long hours of listening to patients the Viennese medical establishment finds merely hysterical and therefore beneath serious attention. The first consulting room of psychoanalysis, before the name exists, is a rented office and a doctor's patience.

stops.name: Wandsbek, near Hamburg: the marriage to Martha Bernays
stops.campa: After a four-year engagement of poverty, jealousy, and nine hundred surviving letters, Freud marries Martha Bernays at the Wandsbek town hall, civilly, because Austrian law will not otherwise recognize the union; the religious rite follows the next day at the Wandsbek synagogue under Rabbi Hanover. Fourteen guests attend; the wedding dinner is taken at Hirschel's Hotel. They honeymoon briefly at Travemünde on the Baltic before returning to Vienna, where Martha will bear him six children in nine years and run the household that makes Berggasse 19 possible.

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: moving in
stops.campa: The family, Martha, the children Mathilde, Martin, and infant Oliver, moves into a newly built apartment house on the Berggasse in Vienna's ninth district, taking rooms on the mezzanine and, from 1896, an office on the floor below when space runs short. Freud will keep this address for nearly forty-seven years: the couch, the study crowded with antiquities, the consulting-room door through which two generations of patients and disciples will pass. Nothing yet marks it as sacred ground. It is simply where a struggling nerve-doctor and his young family have found an affordable, respectable flat.

stops.name: Schloss Bellevue, near Grinzing: the secret of the dream
stops.campa: Summering at the Schloss Bellevue restaurant on the Kahlenberg slope above Grinzing, Freud dreams that his patient Irma stands before him with a throat full of white patches, and Dr. M. and two colleagues examine her while a formula for trimethylamin hovers absurdly in the air. Waking, he sees the dream not as nonsense but as a disguised wish, to be innocent of Irma's continuing illness, and begins the analysis that will anchor his whole theory of dreams. He writes to Fliess, half joking, that a marble plaque should someday mark this house as the place where the riddle of dreaming first gave up its secret.
stops.quote: In this house, on July 24th, 1895, the secret of the dream revealed itself to Dr. Sigm. Freud.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Wilhelm Fliess, 12 June 1900, imagining a future plaque

stops.name: Vienna: the death of Jakob Freud
stops.campa: Jakob Freud dies at eighty-one after a long decline, and his son is astonished by the depth of the grief that follows: grief mixed with something more troubling, a self-reproach he cannot at first name. In the months after the funeral Freud turns his new method of dream-analysis on his own dreams and memories, uncovering in himself the hostile wishes toward the father and the desire for the mother that he will soon name, borrowing from Sophocles, the Oedipus complex. The self-analysis undertaken at his father's grave becomes the foundation stone no other analyst's training will ever quite repeat.
stops.quote: By the time he died, his life had been over long before, but at a death the whole past stirs within one.
